front: The electronic configuration of chlorine is 2,8,7. This tells us chlorine is in Period **..........** and Group **..........** .
back: The electronic configuration of chlorine is 2,8,7. This tells us chlorine is in Period **3** and Group **7**.

front:
**True or False?**

Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electron shells.
back:
**False.**

Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their **outer shell**, not the same number of shells.

front: What is a metalloid (semi-metal)?
back: A **metalloid** is an element that shows properties of both **metals and non-metals**. Metalloids lie between the metals and non-metals on the Periodic Table.

front: Lithium has the electronic configuration 2,1. Sodium has 2,8,1. Both are in Group 1 because they each have **..........** electron(s) in their **..........** shell.
back: Lithium has the electronic configuration 2,1. Sodium has 2,8,1. Both are in Group 1 because they each have **1** electron(s) in their **outer** shell.

front: Why do metals form basic oxides while non-metals form acidic oxides?
back:
Metals tend to lose electrons and react with acids, so their oxides are **basic**.

Non-metals tend to gain electrons and their oxides dissolve in water to give **acidic** solutions.

front: How does the reactivity of Group 1 metals change going down the group, based on the observations of lithium, sodium and potassium with water?
back: Reactivity **increases** going down Group 1. Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium, which reacts more vigorously than lithium.

front: Why are Group I metals called the alkali metals?
back: They are called alkali metals because they react with water to form **alkaline solutions** with a high pH.

front: Group I metals react with water to produce a metal **..........** solution and **..........** gas.
back: Group I metals react with water to produce a metal **hydroxide** solution and **hydrogen** gas.

front:
**True or False?**

Reactivity of Group I metals decreases as you go down the group.
back:
**False.**

Reactivity of Group I metals **increases** going down the group, so potassium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium.

front: Why are Group I metals stored under oil?
back: Group I metals are stored under oil to prevent them from reacting with **oxygen and water vapour** in the air.

front: Going down Group I, melting point **..........** and reactivity with water **..........** .
back: Going down Group I, melting point **decreases** and reactivity with water **increases**.

front: What is the distinguishing observation when potassium reacts with water, compared with sodium?
back: Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium and burns with a **lilac flame** on the surface of the water.

front: Why does reactivity increase going down Group I?
back: Reactivity increases because the **outer electron** is further from the nucleus in each successive element, so it is **more easily lost** when the metal reacts.

front: Define **diatomic**.
back: **Diatomic** means consisting of two atoms bonded together. All halogens exist as diatomic molecules, e.g. Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.

front: At room temperature, chlorine is a **..........** gas, bromine is a **..........** liquid and iodine is a **..........** solid.
back: At room temperature, chlorine is a **pale yellow-green** gas, bromine is a **red-brown** liquid and iodine is a **grey-black** solid.

front:
**True or False?**

Reactivity of Group VII elements increases going down the group.
back:
**False.**

Reactivity of Group VII elements **decreases** going down the group, because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and harder to attract an incoming electron.

front: Why does reactivity decrease going down Group VII?
back: Going down Group VII, the **atomic radius** increases and there is greater **electron shielding**, so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly and it becomes harder to gain the outer electron needed to react.

front: Going down Group VII, melting point **..........** , density **..........** and colour becomes **..........** .
back: Going down Group VII, melting point **increases**, density **increases** and colour becomes **darker**.

front: What charge does a **halide ion** carry?
back: A halide ion carries a **1−** charge.

front: What are the three colours of iodine in its different forms: solid, vapour and aqueous solution?
back: Solid iodine is **grey-black**, iodine vapour is **purple** and aqueous iodine is **brown**.

front: Which Group VII elements exist as diatomic molecules?
back: All Group VII elements are diatomic: **F**<sub>**2**</sub> (fluorine), **Cl**<sub>**2**</sub> (chlorine), **Br**<sub>**2**</sub> (bromine) and **I**<sub>**2**</sub> (iodine).

front: How is a **halide ion** formed from a halogen atom?
back: A halide ion is formed when a halogen atom **gains one electron** to complete its outer shell of eight electrons, giving it a **1−** charge.

front: What is a halogen displacement reaction?
back: A halogen displacement reaction is one in which a **more reactive halogen** displaces a **less reactive halogen** from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

front: When Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) is added to KBr (aq), the solution turns **..........** because **..........** is displaced.
back: When Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) is added to KBr (aq), the solution turns **orange** because **bromine** is displaced.

front:
**True or False?**

Iodine can displace bromine from a solution of potassium bromide.
back:
**False.**

Iodine is **less reactive** than bromine, so it cannot displace bromine. Only a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one.

front: Why can chlorine displace bromide ions from solution?
back: Chlorine is **more reactive** than bromine so it can **oxidise** bromide ions, gaining electrons to form chloride ions and releasing bromine.

front:
The ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromide ions is:

2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) →  (aq) +  (aq)
back:
The ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromide ions is:

2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) → **2Cl**<sup>**-**</sup> (aq) + **Br**<sub>**2**</sub> (aq)

front: What colour change is observed when bromine solution is added to potassium iodide solution, and what does this indicate?
back: The solution turns **brown**, indicating that bromine has displaced iodide ions to form **iodine**, I<sub>2</sub>, which is more reactive than iodine.

front: How does reactivity order of chlorine, bromine and iodine determine the outcome of a displacement reaction?
back: **Chlorine** is the most reactive and **iodine** the least. A halogen will only displace a halide ion that is lower in reactivity, so chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide while bromine only displaces iodide.

front: Where are the transition elements found in the Periodic Table?
back: Transition elements are found in the **central block** of the Periodic Table, between Group 2 and Group 3.

front: Transition elements form ions with **..........** charges, produce **..........** compounds and are useful as **..........** .
back: Transition elements form ions with **variable** charges, produce **coloured** compounds and are useful as **catalysts**.

front:
**True or False?**

All transition elements have high melting points.
back:
**False.**

Most transition elements have high melting points, but **mercury** is an exception: it has a low melting point and is a liquid at room temperature.

front: What two oxidation states does iron commonly form, and what is the significance of transition elements having variable oxidation states?
back: Iron forms **Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup> and **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup> ions. **Variable oxidation states** are a key property of transition elements and distinguish them from most other metals.

front: CuSO<sub>4</sub> solution is **..........** in colour, showing that copper forms **..........** compounds.
back: CuSO<sub>4</sub> solution is **blue** in colour, showing that copper forms **coloured** compounds.

front: Why are transition elements widely used as industrial catalysts?
back: Transition elements are effective catalysts because they can form ions with **variable oxidation states**, allowing them to accept and donate electrons during a reaction.

front: Why are scandium and zinc not classed as transition elements, despite being in the transition element region of the table?
back: Scandium and zinc are not classed as transition elements because they do not form **coloured compounds** and each has only **one oxidation state**.

front: Why are the noble gases described as inert?
back: Noble gases are inert because they have **full outer shells** of electrons, making their electronic configurations extremely stable and leaving no tendency to gain or lose electrons.

front: Helium has the electronic configuration **..........** and neon has the configuration **..........** , both giving a full outer shell.
back: Helium has the electronic configuration **2** and neon has the configuration **2,8**, both giving a full outer shell.

front:
**True or False?**

Noble gases are diatomic molecules.
back:
**False.**

Noble gases are **monoatomic**, meaning each particle consists of a single atom.

front: Why do noble gases not form bonds with other elements?
back: Noble gases do not form bonds because their **outer shells are already full**, so they have no need to gain or lose electrons to achieve stability.

front: The noble gases are located in Group **..........** of the Periodic Table and are all **..........** at room temperature.
back: The noble gases are located in Group **VIII** of the Periodic Table and are all **gaseous** at room temperature.

front: How many electrons does argon have in its outer shell, and how does this explain its lack of reactivity?
back: Argon has **8 electrons** in its outer shell. This **full outer shell** means argon has no tendency to gain or lose electrons, so it does not react.
